claim: Motor units transduce neural signals from supraspinal centres, spinal circuits, and sensory systems into force.
source: Motor units transduce the neural signals that originate from supraspinal centres, spinal circuits, and sensory systems into force (Sherrington, 1925).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sherrington, 1925

claim: In healthy individuals, each action potential propagating along the axon of an alpha motor neuron elicits action potentials in all its innervated muscle fibres.
source: In healthy individuals, each action potential propagating along the axon of an alpha motor neuron elicits action potentials in all its innervated muscle fibres.
evidence: Based on established neuroscience knowledge about motor neuron function

claim: The activity of motor neurons represents the neural code of movement to muscles.
source: The activity of motor neuron – in the form of spike trains – represents the neural code of movement to muscles.
evidence: Based on established understanding of motor control

claim: Decoding motor neuron firing activity in real time during various behaviours can substantially enhance understanding of movement control.
source: Decoding this firing activity in real time during various behaviours can thus substantially enhance our understanding of movement control (Basmajian, 1963; Formento et al., 2021; Bräcklein et al., 2022; Rossato et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work

claim: Real-time decoding of motor neurons is essential for interfacing with external devices.
source: Real-time decoding is also essential for interfacing with external devices (Farina et al., 2023) or virtual limbs (Oliveira et al., 2024) when activity is present at the periphery of the nervous system.
evidence: Supported by citations to Farina et al., 2023 and Oliveira et al., 2024

claim: Individuals with spinal cord injury can control a virtual hand with residual firing activity of motor units in their forearm.
source: For example, individuals with a spinal cord injury can control a virtual hand with the residual firing activity of the motor units in their forearm (Oliveira et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oliveira et al., 2024

claim: Individuals can intuitively learn to independently control motor units within the same muscle using visual cues.
source: In this way, Formento et al., 2021 showed that individuals can intuitively learn to independently control motor units within the same muscle using visual cues.
evidence: Supported by citation to Formento et al., 2021

claim: Researchers classically identify a few motor units during relatively weak contractions using concentric needle or fine wire recording electrodes.
source: To date, researchers classically identify a few motor units during relatively weak contractions using concentric needle or fine wire recording electrodes (LeFever and De Luca, 1982).
evidence: Supported by citation to LeFever and De Luca, 1982

claim: Recent developments of intramuscular and surface EMG electrode arrays facilitate both a larger recording zone and the recording of the same motor unit action potential across multiple channels.
source: Recent developments of intramuscular (Farina et al., 2008b; Muceli et al., 2015; Muceli et al., 2022; Chung et al., 2023) and surface (Farina et al., 2016; Caillet et al., 2023) electromyography (EMG) electrode arrays facilitate both a larger recording zone (i.e. the volume from which motor unit action potentials are recorded), and the recording of the same motor unit action potential across multiple channels.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work on electrode arrays

claim: Blind-source separation algorithms enable a relatively large number of individual motor units to be decoded from each recording.
source: In conjunction with this hardware advance, the development of novel EMG decomposition software/programs, such as multichannel spike-sorting (Rey et al., 2015; Buccino et al., 2020; Steinmetz et al., 2021; Pachitariu et al., 2023) and blind-source separation (Holobar and Zazula, 2007; Holobar and Farina, 2014; Farina and Holobar, 2016; Negro et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2019) algorithms, enables a relatively large number of individual motor units to be decoded from each recording (Muceli et al., 2015; Muceli et al., 2022; Chung et al., 2023; Caillet et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work

claim: Blind-source separation optimises a set of separation vectors (motor unit filters) which maximises the sparseness of motor unit pulse trains from which discharge times are estimated.
source: Contrary to spike-sorting algorithms, blind-source separation does not directly sort action potential shapes, but rather optimises a set of separation vectors, that is, motor unit filters, which maximises the sparseness of motor unit pulse trains from which discharge times are estimated (Holobar and Zazula, 2007; Holobar and Farina, 2014; Farina and Holobar, 2016; Negro et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations describing the method

claim: Current open-source implementations of blind-source separation rely on offline processing.
source: The current open-source implementations of this approach rely on offline processing, which restricts its ability to be used for neurofeedback and human interfacing technologies.
evidence: Based on assessment of available software implementations

claim: Recent studies have reported real-time capabilities of motor unit identification by adapting the offline blind-source separation algorithm using a two-step approach.
source: Recent studies have reported real-time capabilities of motor unit identification by adapting the offline blind-source separation algorithm (Formento et al., 2021; Bräcklein et al., 2022; Barsakcioglu et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2020; Zheng and Hu, 2019). These studies used a two-step approach: (1) the separation vector for each motor unit is identified with offline decomposition during the training phase and (2) the same vectors are applied in real time to new EMG recordings.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work

claim: There are no publicly available algorithms or user interfaces for real-time motor unit identification.
source: The real-time identification of motor units is only used by a few specialised research teams, and there are no publicly available algorithms or user interfaces for this task.
evidence: Based on assessment of available software

claim: The accuracy and capabilities of online decomposition have not been systematically tested in multiple muscles or intensities.
source: In addition, the accuracy and capabilities of online decomposition have not been systematically tested in multiple muscles or intensities.
evidence: Based on review of prior literature

claim: The study provides an open-source software that can be used to visualise and track motor unit firing activities in real time.
source: Here, we provide an open-source software that can be used to visualise and track motor unit firing activities in real time.
evidence: Direct statement of the study's contribution

claim: The software validity was documented on data collected from five lower limb muscles using either surface or intramuscular electrode arrays.
source: We document the software validity and its capabilities on data collected from five lower limb muscles (gastrocnemius lateralis and medialis, vastus lateralis and medialis, and tibialis anterior) during isometric contractions of varying force levels, using either surface or intramuscular electrode arrays.
evidence: Description of experimental validation performed in the study

claim: The real-time identification of motor unit firing activity was first validated using synthetic EMG signals.
source: The real-time identification of motor unit firing activity was first validated using synthetic EMG signals.
evidence: Description of validation approach used in the study

claim: Data, codes, and a user manual are available at https://github.com/simonavrillon/I-Spin.
source: Data, codes, and a user manual are available at https://github.com/simonavrillon/I-Spin (copy archived at Avrillon, 2024).
evidence: Direct statement about data availability

claim: During stationary conditions, the train of motor unit action potentials can be modelled as the convolution of series of discrete delta functions representing discharge times and motor unit action potentials that have a consistent shape across time.
source: During stationary conditions, for example, isometric contractions, the train of motor unit action potentials can be modelled as the convolution of series of discrete delta functions, representing the discharge times, and motor unit action potentials that have a consistent shape across time.
evidence: Based on established signal processing models for EMG

claim: The shape of the recorded potential of each motor unit differs across electrodes due to varying conduction velocity of action potentials among muscle fibres and the location/depth of muscle fibres relative to electrodes.
source: When EMG signals are recorded with an array of electrodes, the shape of the recorded potential of each motor unit differs across electrodes. This is due to (1) the varying conduction velocity of action potentials among the muscle fibres and (2) the location/depth of the muscle fibres that belong to each motor unit relatively to the electrodes, which impact the low pass filtering effect of the tissue on the recorded potential.
evidence: Based on established biophysics of EMG signal generation

claim: Increasing the number and density of recording electrodes increases the likelihood that each motor unit will have a unique motor unit action potential profile.
source: Increasing the number and density of recording electrodes increases the likelihood that each motor unit will have a unique motor unit action potential profile (shape), that is, a temporal and spatial profile that differs from all the other active motor unit within the recorded volume (Caillet et al., 2023; Farina et al., 2008a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Caillet et al., 2023 and Farina et al., 2008a

claim: The uniqueness of motor unit action potential profiles is necessary for blind-source separation to accurately estimate motor unit discharge times.
source: The uniqueness of motor unit action potential profiles is necessary for the blind-source separation to accurately estimate the motor unit discharge times.
evidence: Based on understanding of blind-source separation requirements

claim: The spike trains of two motor units with similar action potential profiles will be merged by the model.
source: Conversely, the spike trains of two motor units with similar action potential profiles will be merged by the model.
evidence: Based on understanding of blind-source separation limitations

claim: The software uses fast independent component analysis (fastICA) to retrieve motor unit spike trains from EMG signals.
source: Our software uses a fast independent component analysis (fastICA) to retrieve motor unit spike trains from the EMG signals.
evidence: Description of the algorithm used in the software

claim: The algorithm iteratively optimises a separation vector for each motor unit.
source: For this, it iteratively optimises a separation vector (i.e. the motor unit filter) for each motor unit (Figure 1B; Negro et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2019; Barsakcioglu et al., 2021; Negro et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2019; Barsakcioglu et al., 2021).
evidence: Description of algorithm with reference to Figure 1B and citations

claim: The projection of EMG signals on the separation vector generates a sparse motor unit pulse train.
source: The projection of the EMG signals on this separation vector generates a sparse motor unit pulse train, with most of its samples close to zero and a smaller number of samples significantly greater than zero (Figure 1B).
evidence: Description of algorithm output with reference to Figure 1B

claim: Discharge times are estimated from the motor unit pulse train using a peak detection function and k-mean classification with two classes.
source: The discharge times are estimated from this motor unit pulse train using a peak detection function and a k-mean classification with two classes to separate the high peaks (spikes) from the low peaks (noise and other motor units).
evidence: Description of the discharge time estimation method

claim: During real-time decomposition, short segments of EMG signals are projected on saved separation vectors and peaks are classified as discharge times based on distance to centroids.
source: During the decomposition in real time, short segments of EMG signals are projected on the saved separation vectors, and the peaks are classified as discharge times if they are closer to the centroid of the class 'spikes' than to the centroid of the class 'noise' (Figure 1C).
evidence: Description of real-time algorithm with reference to Figure 1C

claim: The algorithm used to identify motor unit discharge activity is based on that proposed by Negro et al., 2016 and Barsakcioglu et al., 2021.
source: The algorithm used to identify motor units discharge activity is based on that proposed by Negro et al., 2016 and Barsakcioglu et al., 2021.
evidence: Citation to prior work on which the algorithm is based

claim: The software was coded as a MATLAB app (version 2022a) with an alternative Python version also available.
source: The software used in this article was coded as a MATLAB app (version 2022a, The MathWorks, Inc, USA), but an alternative version coded with Python is also available.
evidence: Description of software implementation

claim: The software allows researchers to record and process signals from surface and intramuscular electrode arrays using multiple acquisition systems.
source: It allows researchers to record and process signals from surface and intramuscular electrode arrays using multiple acquisition systems (EMG-Quattrocento, OT Bioelettronica, Italy; Open Ephys acquisition board, Open Ephys, USA; Intan RHD recording system; Intan Technologies, USA).
evidence: Description of software capabilities

claim: It is recommended to record EMG signals during stationary conditions to limit changes in muscle geometry or position/orientation of active muscle fibres relative to electrodes.
source: As the accuracy of the algorithm relies on the consistency of motor unit filters, it is recommended to record these EMG signals during stationary conditions – for example, isometric contractions – to limit changes in muscle geometry or position/orientation of the active muscle fibres relative to the electrodes (Glaser and Holobar, 2019; Oliveira and Negro, 2021).
evidence: Recommendation supported by citations to Glaser and Holobar, 2019 and Oliveira and Negro, 2021

claim: The framework for real-time identification of motor neuron activity has four steps.
source: The framework to perform real-time identification of motor neuron activity has four steps (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Description of the framework with reference to figure

claim: Three forms of feedback can be displayed to the participant: a raster plot, a quadrant displaying firing rates of two motor units, and the smoothed firing rate of a given motor unit with a scrolling target.
source: Three forms of feedback can be displayed to the participant: a raster plot of the discharge times for each motor unit of a given array, a quadrant displaying the firing rates of two motor units, and the smoothed firing rate of a given motor unit with a scrolling target to track (Figure 1C).
evidence: Description of feedback options with reference to Figure 1C

claim: Manual editing of motor unit discharge times identified with automatic decomposition generally improves the accuracy of spike trains.
source: Manual editing of motor unit discharge times identified with automatic decomposition (or spike-sorting) generally improves the accuracy of the spike trains (Del Vecchio et al., 2020; Hug et al., 2021; Avrillon et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to Del Vecchio et al., 2020, Hug et al., 2021, and Avrillon et al., 2024

claim: Manual editing can be performed after the baseline contraction to improve the accuracy of motor unit filters.
source: In the case of online decomposition, manual editing can be performed after the baseline contraction to improve the accuracy of the motor unit filters.
evidence: Description of when manual editing is applied

claim: The silhouette value (SIL) measures the normalised distance between spikes and noise after k-mean classification.
source: For example, the silhouette value (SIL) measures the normalised distance between the spikes and the noise after k-mean classification (Negro et al., 2016).
evidence: Definition of metric supported by citation to Negro et al., 2016

claim: At 20% MVC baseline contractions, on average 20±9 (VL), 14±5 (VM), 25±11 (GL), 19±9 (GM), 15±4 (TA grid), and 10 (TA intra) motor units per participant were identified.
source: When considering the baseline contractions performed at 20% MVC, on average 20 ± 9 (VL), 14 ± 5 (VM), 25 ± 11 (GL), 19 ± 9 (GM), 15 ± 4 (TA grid), and 10 (TA intra) motor units per participant were identified.
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: SIL values before manual editing were 0.89±0.05 for VL, 0.83±0.04 for VM, 0.82±0.03 for GL, 0.87±0.04 for GM, 0.94±0.01 for TAgrid, and 0.95±0.02 for TAintra at 20% MVC.
source: Their SIL values calculated before manual editing were 0.89 ± 0.05 for VL, 0.83 ± 0.04 for VM, 0.82 ± 0.03 for GL, 0.87 ± 0.04 for GM, 0.94 ± 0.01 for TAgrid, and 0.95 ± 0.02 for TAintra.
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: After visual inspection, a significant number of motor units was removed: 6±5 for VL, 10±5 for VM, 21±12 for GL, 6±5 for GM, and 1 for TA grid and TA intra.
source: After visual inspection, a significant number of motor units was removed as their pulse train showed no clear separation between the spikes and the noise. The number of motor units removed was 6 ± 5 for VL, 10 ± 5 for VM, 21 ± 12 for GL, 6 ± 5 for GM, and 1 for TA grid and TA intra (Figure 2A).
evidence: Experimental data from the study with reference to Figure 2A

claim: After manual editing, remaining motor units exhibited SIL values of 0.91±0.04 (VL), 0.89±0.06 (VM), 0.89±0.03 (GL), 0.90±0.02 (GM), 0.94±0.01 (TAgrid), and 0.95±0.02 (TAintra).
source: The remaining motor units exhibited a SIL value of 0.91 ± 0.04, 0.89 ± 0.06, 0.89 ± 0.03, and 0.90 ± 0.02, 0.94 ± 0.01, and 0.95 ± 0.02 for VL, VM, GL, GM, TAgrid, and TA intra, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: Experimental data from the study with reference to Figure 2B

claim: At 40% MVC baseline contractions, on average 17±6 (VL), 15±5 (VM), 29±13 (GL), and 13±4 (GM) motor units were identified by automatic decomposition.
source: When considering the baseline contraction performed at 40% MVC, on average 17 ± 6 (VL), 15 ± 5 (VM), 29 ± 13 (GL), and 13 ± 4 (GM) motor units were identified by automatic decomposition, with 12 ± 8 (VL), 3 ± 3 (VM), 5 ± 6 (GL), and 4 ± 3 (GM) motor units kept after visual inspection (Figure 2A).
evidence: Experimental data from the study with reference to Figure 2A

claim: After manual editing at 40% MVC, SIL values reached 0.91±0.03 for VL, 0.89±0.05 for VM, 0.87±0.02 for GL, and 0.88±0.03 for GM.
source: The SIL value of the selected motor units reached 0.91 ± 0.03 for VL, 0.89 ± 0.05 for VM, 0.87 ± 0.02 for GL, and 0.88 ± 0.03 for GM after manual editing (Figure 2B).
evidence: Experimental data from the study with reference to Figure 2B

claim: A SIL value around 0.9 can be used as a threshold to automatically remove motor unit pulse trains with poor quality a priori.
source: These results show how manual editing can improve the accuracy of spike detection from the motor unit pulse trains. Moreover, a SIL value around 0.9 can be used as a threshold to automatically remove the motor unit pulse trains with a poor quality a priori.
evidence: Inference from the experimental data showing SIL values after editing

claim: The motor unit pulse train must always be visually inspected after the session to check for errors of automatic identification of discharge times.
source: Importantly, it is worth noting that the motor unit pulse train must always be visually inspected after the session to check for errors of the automatic identification of discharge times.
evidence: Recommendation based on understanding of algorithm limitations

claim: Synthetic EMG signals were generated with an anatomical model entailing a cylindrical muscle volume with parallel fibres.
source: We first validated the accuracy of the algorithm using synthetic EMG signals generated with an anatomical model entailing a cylindrical muscle volume with parallel fibres (see Farina et al., 2008a, Konstantin et al., 2020 for a full description of the model).
evidence: Description of simulation method with citations

claim: The simulation model included 150 motor units distributed within the cross-section of the muscle.
source: A total of 150 motor units were distributed within the cross-section of the muscle.
evidence: Description of simulation parameters

claim: Recruitment thresholds, firing rate/excitatory drive relations, and twitch parameters were assigned to each motor unit using the same procedure as Fuglevand et al., 1993.
source: Recruitment thresholds, firing rate/excitatory drive relations, and twitch parameters were assigned to each motor unit using the same procedure as Fuglevand et al., 1993.
evidence: Description of simulation method with citation

claim: On average 10±1 and 12±2 motor units were identified with surface and intramuscular arrays, respectively, in the simulations.
source: We identified on average 10 ± 1 and 12 ± 2 motor units with surface and intramuscular arrays, respectively (Figure 3A).
evidence: Simulation results with reference to Figure 3A

claim: During offline decomposition of synthetic signals, the rate of agreement reached 100.0±0.0% for intramuscular EMG signals and 99.2±1.8% for surface EMG signals.
source: During the offline decomposition, the rate of agreement between the identified discharge times and the ground truth, that is, the simulated discharge times, reached 100.0 ± 0.0% for intramuscular EMG signals and 99.2 ± 1.8% for surface EMG signals (Figure 3B).
evidence: Simulation results with reference to Figure 3B

claim: The offline estimation of motor unit filters was highly accurate, independently of the level of force or the pattern of the isometric contraction.
source: The offline estimation of motor unit filters was therefore highly accurate, independently of the level of force or the pattern of the isometric contraction.
evidence: Inference from simulation results

claim: When motor unit filters from 20% MVC were applied in real time on sinusoidal contraction signals, rates of agreement reached 96.3±4.6% (surface) and 98.4±2.3% (intramuscular).
source: Motor unit filters estimated during a baseline contraction at 20% MVC were then applied in real time on signals simulated during a contraction with a different pattern (sinusoidal; Figure 3C). The rates of agreement between the online decomposition and the ground truth reached 96.3 ± 4.6% and 98.4 ± 2.3% for surface and intramuscular EMG signals, respectively.
evidence: Simulation results with reference to Figure 3C

claim: When motor unit filters from 20% MVC were applied to signals at 10% MVC, rate of agreement was 99.8±0.2% (surface) and 99.5±0.3% (intramuscular).
source: Finally, we tested whether the accuracy of the online decomposition changed when the level of force decreased or increased by 10% MVC when compared to the calibration performed at 20% MVC (Figure 3D). The rate of agreement remained high when applying the motor unit filters on signals recorded at 10% MVC: 99.8 ± 0.2% (surface EMG) and 99.5 ± 0.3% (intramuscular EMG).
evidence: Simulation results with reference to Figure 3D

claim: Only 3 out of 10 motor units identified from surface EMG at 20% MVC were active at 10% MVC, while 8 out of 12 from intramuscular EMG were active at 10% MVC.
source: It is worth noting that only 3 out of 10 motor units identified from surface EMG at 20% MVC were active at 10% MVC, while 8 out of 12 motor units identified from intramuscular EMG were active at 10% MVC.
evidence: Simulation results

claim: EMG decomposition tends to identify the last recruited motor units, which often innervate a larger number of fibres than early recruited motor units.
source: This shows how the decomposition of EMG signals tends to identify the last recruited motor units, which often innervate a larger number of fibres than the early recruited motor units (Henneman, 1957).
evidence: Inference from simulation data supported by citation to Henneman, 1957

claim: When motor unit filters from 20% MVC were applied to signals at 30% MVC, rate of agreement decreased to 88.6±14.0% (surface) and 80.3±19.2% (intramuscular).
source: On the contrary, the application of motor unit filters on signals simulated at 30% MVC led to a decrease in the rate of agreement, with values of 88.6 ± 14.0% (surface EMG) and 80.3 ± 19.2% (intramuscular EMG).
evidence: Simulation results

claim: The decrease in accuracy at 30% MVC was caused by the recruitment of two motor units sharing a similar space within the muscle, resulting in a merge in the same pulse train.
source: For the other motor units, we observed a decrease in precision, which estimates the ratio of true discharge times over the total number of identified discharge times. This was caused by the recruitment of two motor units sharing a similar space within the muscle, which resulted in a merge in the same pulse train (Figure 3D).
evidence: Explanation of simulation results with reference to Figure 3D

claim: Eight participants (four males and four females) performed trapezoidal isometric contractions at 10 and 20% MVC with surface EMG recorded from TA with 256 electrodes.
source: We then asked eight participants (four males and four females) to perform trapezoidal isometric contractions with plateaus of force set at 10 and 20% MVC during which surface EMG signals were recorded from the TA with 256 electrodes separated by 4 mm.
evidence: Description of experimental procedure

claim: A total of 144 motor units were identified at both 10 and 20% MVC in the TA experiment.
source: A total of 144 motor units were identified at both 10 and 20% MVC.
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: When test signals were recorded at the same force level as baseline, rates of agreement were 95.6±6.8% (10% MVC) and 93.9±5.9% (20% MVC).
source: When the test signals were recorded at the same level of force as the baseline contraction, we obtained rates of agreement of 95.6 ± 6.8% (10% MVC) and 93.9 ± 5.9% (20% MVC).
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: Sensitivity reached 95.9±6.7% (10% MVC) and 94.4±5.6% (20% MVC) when test and baseline forces matched.
source: The sensitivity reached 95.9 ± 6.7% (10% MVC) and 94.4 ± 5.6% (20% MVC), and the precision reached 99.6 ± 1.3% (10% MVC) and 99.4 ± 1.9% (20% MVC).
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: Precision reached 99.6±1.3% (10% MVC) and 99.4±1.9% (20% MVC) when test and baseline forces matched.
source: The sensitivity reached 95.9 ± 6.7% (10% MVC) and 94.4 ± 5.6% (20% MVC), and the precision reached 99.6 ± 1.3% (10% MVC) and 99.4 ± 1.9% (20% MVC).
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: When filters from 20% MVC were applied to signals at 10% MVC, rate of agreement decreased to 87.9±16.2%.
source: When the filters identified at 20% MVC were applied on signals recorded at a lower level of force (10% MVC), the rates of agreement decreased to 87.9 ± 16.2%.
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: When filters from 20% MVC were applied to signals at 10% MVC, sensitivity decreased to 88.0±16.2% but precision remained high at 99.4±4.3%.
source: The sensitivity also decreased to 88.0 ± 16.2%, but the precision remained high (99.4 ± 4.3).
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: The decrease in accuracy when applying 20% MVC filters to 10% MVC signals was mostly caused by missed discharge times rather than false identification of artefacts or spikes from other motor units.
source: Thus, the decrease in accuracy was mostly caused by missed discharge times rather than the false identification of artefacts or spikes from other motor units.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing high precision but lower sensitivity

claim: When filters from 10% MVC were applied to signals at 20% MVC, rate of agreement decreased to 83.3±13.5%.
source: When the filters identified at 10% MVC were applied to signals recorded at a higher level of force, the rates of agreement decreased to 83.3 ± 13.5%.
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: When filters from 10% MVC were applied to signals at 20% MVC, sensitivity decreased to 90.7±8.1% and precision decreased to 90.9±12.6%.
source: The sensitivity decreased to 90.7 ± 8.1%, and the precision also decreased to 90.9 ± 12.6%.
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: Motor units recruited between 10 and 20% MVC can substantially disrupt the accuracy of real-time decomposition.
source: This result confirms what was observed with synthetic EMG, that is, motor units recruited between 10 and 20% MVC can substantially disrupt the accuracy of the decomposition in real time, as highlighted in Figure 4 (lower panel).
evidence: Inference from experimental data with reference to Figure 4

claim: Twenty-one male participants completed experiments to test the accuracy of online decomposition in different muscles.
source: Twenty-one male participants completed additional experiments to test the accuracy of the online decomposition in different muscles (vastus lateralis [VL] and medialis [VM], gastrocnemius lateralis [GL] and medialis [GM], and tibialis anterior [TA]).
evidence: Description of experimental procedure

claim: At 20% MVC, 94 (VL), 21 (VM), 14 (GL), 56 (GM), 68 (TA grid), and 9 (TA intra) motor units were identified.
source: At 20% MVC, 94 (VL; eight participants), 21 (VM; eight participants), 14 (GL; eight participants), 56 (GM; eight participants), 68 (TA grid; five participants), and 9 motor units (TA intra; one participant) motor units were identified.
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: At 40% MVC, 76 (VL), 21 (VM), 19 (GL), and 25 (GM) motor units were identified.
source: At 40% MVC, 76 (VL), 21 (VM), 19 (GL), and 25 (GM) motor units were identified.
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: The highest rate of agreement was observed for TA (93.6±9.2% with grid and 97.3±5.2% with intramuscular array).
source: The highest rate of agreement was observed for the TA (93.6 ± 9.2% with the grid and 97.3 ± 5.2% with the intramuscular array).
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: Rates of agreement were lower for vastii (VL: 82.1±19.7%; VM: 75.3±18.5%) and gastrocnemii muscles (GL: 88.1±7.8%; GM: 81.0±17.7%).
source: Those values were lower for the vastii (VL: 82.1 ± 19.7%; VM: 75.3 ± 18.5%) and gastrocnemii muscles (GL: 88.1 ± 7.8%; GM: 81.0 ± 17.7).
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: At 40% MVC, rate of agreement was 84.0±15.6% for VL, 75.2±20.6% for VM, 82.5±8.1% for GL, and 87.9±8.7% for GM.
source: When considering the contractions performed at 40% MVC, the rate of agreement was 84.0 ± 15.6% for VL, 75.2 ± 20.6% for VM, 82.5 ± 8.1% for GL, and 87.9 ± 8.7% for GM (Figure 5).
evidence: Experimental data from the study with reference to Figure 5

claim: At 20% MVC, the RMSE between real-time and edited firing rates was consistently below two pulses per second for all motor units.
source: At 20% MVC, the root mean squared error (RMSE) between the firing rate estimated in real time and its edited version was consistently below two pulses per second for all the motor units (Figure 6).
evidence: Experimental data from the study with reference to Figure 6

claim: The lowest RMSE was observed with TA muscle (0.64±0.77 pps with grids and 0.44±0.43 pps with intramuscular arrays).
source: The lowest RMSE was observed with the TA muscle (0.64 ± 0.77 pps and 0.44 ± 0.43 pps with grids and intramuscular arrays of electrodes).
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: At 20% MVC, RMSE was 1.4±1.5 pps for VL, 1.8±1.5 pps for VM, 1.7±1.1 pps for GL, and 1.1±1.1 pps for GM.
source: RMSE was 1.4 ± 1.5 pps for VL, 1.8 ± 1.5 pps for VM, 1.7 ± 1.1 pps for GL, and 1.1 ± 1.1 pps for GM.
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: At 40% MVC, RMSE reached 1.1±1.2 pps for VL, 1.8±1.1 pps for VM, 0.8±0.5 pps for GL, and 0.6±0.4 pps for GM.
source: At 40% MVC, the RMSE reached 1.1 ± 1.2 pps for VL, 1.8 ± 1.1 pps for VM, 0.8 ± 0.5 pps for GL, and 0.6 ± 0.4 pps for GM.
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: The RMSE values provide strong evidence that the biofeedback accurately reflects motor unit firing activity.
source: Overall, these RMSE provides strong evidence that the biofeedback accurately reflects the motor unit firing activity.
evidence: Inference from experimental RMSE data

claim: The most important assumption for blind-source separation is the uniqueness of the distribution of motor unit action potentials across electrodes among all active motor units.
source: There are processing assumptions for the blind-source separation algorithm to accurately identify motor unit discharge times from multichannel EMG signals. Among them, the most important is the uniqueness of the distribution of motor unit action potentials across electrodes (that defines the separation vector) among all the other active motor units within the recording volume (Caillet et al., 2023; Farina et al., 2008a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Caillet et al., 2023 and Farina et al., 2008a
